newsitem.title: USA: Real Christmas tree prices stable, industry rebounds.
newsitem.headline: Real Christmas tree prices stable, industry rebounds.

text.p: Real Christmas trees have apparently overcome an image problem and are again in demand by nostalgic baby boomers.
Growers expect to sell 37 million trees in the United States this season -- 4 million more than in 1994 -- and say consumers can expect to pay about the same amount per tree as last year.
"From what we've heard so far demand is looking good," said Jeff Bender, spokesman for 1,800-member National Christmas Tree Association.

Most retail sales do not begin until after the Thanksgiving holiday, but wholesalers in growing regions such as California, North Carolina, Wisconsin, New England and Pennsylvania have been shipping trees for several weeks.

The tradition of decorating trees for the Christmas season dates back to 16th century Europe, and was introduced to the United States by German settlers and Hessian mercenaries of the Revolutionary War.

Sales of real trees in the United States had been slumping with surveys showing many consumers were switching to artificial trees partly out of concern that forests were being hurt by the mass harvesting of live trees.
Growers countered with educational campaigns on how to recycle trees after the holiday season, and by spreading the word that most trees are actually grown on farms not cut in the wild.
"Growing a Christmas tree is no different than growing corn except that it takes eight years to grow that (tree) crop," said Albert Gondeck, owner of North Parish Tree Farm in Turner, Maine.
Sales of real trees have also benefited from parental nostalgia, according to growers.
"Baby boomers are tending to go to real trees again," said Bender. "They have children (and) they want their children to experience the holidays as they experienced them."

Gondeck's farm is one of many that plays on the nostalgia by allowing customers to cut their own trees. Other growers have tapped baby boomer's hi-tech interests by taking orders through the Internet.
Balsam fir, Scotch pine, Douglas fir, Fraser fir, White pine and Norway spruce continue to be amoung the most popular Christmas tree varieties, according to growers.

According to the National Christmas Tree Association the average retail price for trees will range between $3.50 and $5.65 per foot of tree -- the same as it was in 1995 and 1994. The average sale-height for a tree is six feet two metres.

In addition to enjoying increased demand, the industry appears to have recovered from "a glut" of trees produced by an increase in the number new growers entering the market in the 1980, according to Bender.
"There's been a weeding out," said Bender. "The more serious growers are the ones that are left in the business right now."
Gondeck, who use to grow corn on the central Maine farm where he now raises Balsam firs, cautions against anyone jumping into the growing business based on this latest sales recovery.
"It's not something you want to get into (as) a one crop thing. Remember, first you've got to wait the eight years to sell them," he said.

Bender said real trees still face tough competition from their artificial counterparts, but he disputes the idea that plastic and metal trees last forever. "Our surveys show they are replaced every 10 years," he said.
